exchanges.question: How will deposit competition unfold as AI cash tools like JPM's become widespread, given the risk of deposit pressure and higher betas? On the Basel III reproposal, does the guidance contemplate RWA mitigation and how much SCB relief could come from removing double counting in markets and operational risk?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: the cash tool is at early stages and is about helping clients manage money; it may squeeze margin or create competition somewhere, which is life. Barnum: it is not live yet, targeted at a very small subset of clients with investments; treat it as an experiment. On Basel, Barnum said this is not an optimization story; targeted RWA clarifications are needed (high-yield repo collateral, advised lines) and G-SIB is the key disincentive; because JPM is currently below the floor, removing double counting via stress testing would have no impact, while modifying the operational risk RWA calculation might; he supports removal but it is not the top priority. Dimon: global market shock and operational risk capital are out of whack with reality; JPM already holds $80 billion or $90 billion for trading books.

exchanges.question: Why was NII ex-Markets held at $95 billion despite higher rates and asset sensitivity? If there is a recession and higher defaults in private credit and leveraged lending, what is the ultimate loss to banks and would a default cycle be systemic?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: the EAR is $1.8 billion and removal of back-half cuts affects the full-year average by only about 20 basis points, so the upward revision would be quite small and offset by noise and rounding. Dimon: he does not think private credit would be systemic; private credit leveraged lending is about $1.7 trillion, high yield about $1.7 trillion, bank syndicated leveraged loans about $1.7 trillion, investment grade debt $13 trillion and mortgage debt $13 trillion; losses in the next credit cycle will be worse than people expect relative to the scenario, and a surprise industry usually emerges (possibly software).

exchanges.question: How are scenario weights and macro risks factoring into reserve setting? Has the outlook for loan and deposit growth changed given strong Markets-driven balance sheet growth?
exchanges.answer: Weights were unchanged; the weighted average unemployment rate in the allowance fell from 5.8% to 5.6%, a consumer-led tailwind, plus a Home Lending release of about $110 million to $150 million on HPI; wholesale saw builds on loan growth and idiosyncratic downgrades. The company debated adding downside skew and concluded existing conservative bias was sufficient. Balance sheet growth was primarily low-density, seasonal Markets secured financing; card loan growth expectation of 6% or a little more is unchanged; other lines modest growth with Home Lending headwinds from First Republic roll-off; Markets wholesale lending (data center lending) will be opportunistic.

exchanges.question: How resilient are consumer spend and credit if energy prices stay high, and are there cracks? Separately, any signs of bad volatility in trading and what drove the rise in trading assets?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: nothing new; early roll rates, delinquencies, cash buffers and spend all look healthy; gas or energy is about 3% of the typical consumer's expenditure in the portfolio and no visible discretionary trade-down yet; credit health rests on a strong labor market, and bad outcomes in the Middle East could crack it. Dimon added tax refunds are helping. On trading, no bad volatility (gappy low-liquidity markets) beyond pockets; the rise in trading assets was mostly business-as-usual, seasonal, low risk density growth, not capital deployment.

exchanges.question: How much of the $1.7 trillion private credit market is substitution from banks versus credit banks would never have made, can banks recapture share, what is happening with collateral terms, and are spreads improving? Separately, is the 2% consumer deposit growth the start of a return to higher deposit growth?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: the market was partly arbitrage and banks may recapture some, he is not concerned; spreads move around by bank; JPM has always had marking rights on collateral; actual credit has not gotten much worse though there are pockets; underwriting weakness will produce uneven outcomes and some business will come back to banks. Barnum called 'air pocket' a strong word; too early to say deposit growth is back, tax is helping; consumer deposit growth expectation of low to mid single digits is unchanged and will be clearer after tax season; net new checking accounts over 450,000 this quarter; wholesale deposit growth expected to be significantly less robust than last year. Spread levels were not quantified.

exchanges.question: With first-quarter expenses elevated relative to the roughly $105 billion full-year guide, how will the following three quarters come down? Separately, what is the outlook for stablecoins and digital assets, including deposit and payments impact?
exchanges.answer: Barnum discouraged annualizing the quarter given seasonality in revenue-related expense and said JPM does not manage by cutting to hit guidance; given the exceptionally strong Markets and Banking performance one might have expected a guidance raise, and the $105 billion is not a promise but an outcome of business results, with spending above $105 billion if every quarter were this good. On stablecoins, Kinexys and tokenized deposits are being embraced; wholesale payments are already efficient and low margin; on consumer side, paying rewards as a proxy for interest would create regulatory arbitrage and the same product should be regulated the same way.

exchanges.question: Interest-bearing consumer deposit costs fell nicely; what is the opportunity going forward given the forward curve? Remind us of the structure of private credit loans, including advance rates and credit enhancement.
exchanges.answer: Dimon: margin should be about what it is today, give or take a couple of basis points, roughly the same for now; Barnum: yield curve flows through the high-beta portion, little room to price down the low-beta portion. On private credit, Dimon said the analyst was asking for too much information: they are loans on top of leveraged loans, senior, each with different LTVs and triggers, and BDCs have statutory limits. Barnum: portfolios are diversified with conservative advance rates, good underwriting, sector concentration caps and cash flow trapping.

exchanges.question: Is LLM-enabled cyber risk a different level of risk and how prepared is the banking system? On the opportunity side, could AI materially improve long-term efficiency ratio and extend JPM's business perimeter?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: cyber is the largest risk; JPM is very well protected and constantly in contact with government; AI has made it worse and harder, including Mythos which JPM is testing; banks in total are rather well protected, though not everything they rely on is; much of defense is hygiene. Barnum: AI is a continuum that brings both risk and opportunity. On efficiency, Dimon said it is a bad idea to think AI will improve the efficiency ratio because competitors will do the same and benefits pass to the market; AI does create opportunities such as Connected Commerce, fraud and scam reduction, prospecting and AI services to clients.

exchanges.question: Why has trading been so consistently strong across environments, including this quarter's commodity, rates, credit and equity shocks? Any updated thoughts on capital allocation and buybacks given the large buffer?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: traders do an excellent job, buying and selling almost $4 trillion a day; volume and volatility help by widening spreads; being on the wrong side of a trade is a cost of doing business. Barnum: JPM is deploying much more capital in Markets and returns are good but below the 17% company average. On capital, Dimon said excess capital is around $40 billion today, subject to rules; the preference is to deploy it serving clients over time (more bankers, global banking, branches) and not rush; buybacks only when at a real discount; he would like to remove the line cash returned to investors.

exchanges.question: Can big public banks finance long-duration capital needs or does it go to private markets, and how does higher-for-longer rates affect direct-lending BB and B credits refinancing? Can you size private credit exposure?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: of the $330 billion NBFI in the call report, about $160 billion is core NBFI, of which about $50 billion is private credit (leveraged loan investors); the leveraged loan and back leverage exposure people care about is about $60 billion. Dimon: banks will not warehouse very long-dated assets; private and public markets will converge; with stagflation, higher rates and wider spreads there would be stress for leveraged companies refinancing, not an immediate disaster; a credit cycle will be worse than people think but he does not think it is systemic.

exchanges.question: Has the investment banking pipeline been pushed out or paused given the Middle East? Is the G-SIB surcharge impinging on the ability to grow Markets balance sheet, up over 20% y/y?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: activity held up well in March, partly because of accelerated M&A closings from faster regulatory approvals; the pipeline is resilient, maybe surprisingly so, though derailment in the Middle East would impact sentiment and deal decisions. On G-SIB, the short answer is yes: it disproportionately accrues to Markets and to the low-risk-density business clients want, and JPM will find ways to reduce the charge, which he calls arbitrage and dislikes.

exchanges.question: How does JPMorgan ensure it selects top-tier credits and stays away from weak ones in private credit?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: JPM is disciplined on credit; it turns down loans where it does not like covenants, underwriting or the ability to move assets out of the secured company, and is willing to let its balance sheet shrink; the loan book could drop 10% next year and he would be fine if the loans walked away from were irresponsible.
